name: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges
description: A review paper critically examining the current state of Visual Question Answering (VQA) in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets (DAQUAR, COCO-QA, The VQA Dataset, FM-IQA, Visual7W, Visual Genome, SHAPES), evaluation metrics, and algorithms. The paper discusses limitations of current datasets with regard to their ability to properly train and assess VQA algorithms, exhaustively reviews existing algorithms, and discusses possible future directions for VQA and image understanding research.
creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan, Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science, Rochester Institute of Technology
citeAs: Kafle, K. and Kanan, C. Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges. Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY, 14623.
rai:dataCollection: Multiple VQA datasets were collected using different methods: DAQUAR used images from NYU-DepthV2 Dataset with manually and automatically generated QA pairs; COCO-QA used an NLP algorithm to derive QA pairs from COCO image captions; The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA) used Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to generate questions and answers for COCO images; FM-IQA collected human-generated questions and answers in Chinese with English translations for COCO images; Visual Genome used crowdsourced dense image annotations with both free-form and region-specific question prompting; Visual7W is a subset of Visual Genome; SHAPES consists of programmatically generated questions about synthetic shape images.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, User-generated content data, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The English version of the FM-IQA dataset was unavailable from the provided download link at the time of the review.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images sourced from: NYU-DepthV2 Dataset (DAQUAR), Microsoft COCO dataset with 328,000 images (COCO-QA, COCO-VQA, FM-IQA, Visual7W), COCO and YFCC100M/Flickr100M (Visual Genome), synthetic cartoon images (SYNTH-VQA), and programmatically generated shape images (SHAPES). QA pairs were generated either manually by human annotators or automatically via NLP algorithms.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Datasets released beginning in 2014; the review covers datasets available as of the article's writing.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For COCO-QA, an NLP algorithm derived QA pairs from COCO image captions by breaking sentences into smaller chunks. For SYNTH-VQA, synthetic scenes were constructed from over 100 different objects, 30 animal models, and 20 human cartoon models with deformable limbs and eight facial expressions spanning different age, gender, and races. For Visual Genome, region-specific question prompting was used alongside free-form questions to reduce bias. The VQA Dataset multiple-choice format includes correct answers, plausible answers (collected without seeing the image), popular answers (top 10 most popular), and random answers.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: COCO-VQA questions were split into training (248,349), validation (121,512), and testing (244,302) sets. For evaluation, answers were processed using consensus-based metrics requiring agreement among multiple annotators. DAQUAR is also available in a reduced configuration (DAQUAR-37) with only 37 object categories.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For COCO-VQA, Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were asked to 'Stump a smart robot' to generate questions, and a separate pool of workers generated answers; each question received 10 independent answers. For DAQUAR, additional ground truth answers were collected to create DAQUAR-consensus with an average of 5 human annotated ground truth answers per question. For Visual Genome, annotators used both free-form and region-specific prompting methods to generate QA pairs. For Visual7W, plausible multiple-choice answers were collected by prompting annotators to answer without seeing the image. FM-IQA used human judges to assess answer quality on a 3-point scale (0=totally wrong, 1=partially correct, 2=perfectly correct).
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) was used for COCO-VQA annotation.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is approximately 83.3% using the AccuracyVQA metric. Over 59% of 'Why' questions have less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer. More than 13% of yes/no answers have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators. Simple questions can also evoke diverse answers. The consensus-based evaluation metric awards full score if the algorithm agrees with 3 or more out of 10 annotators.
rai:annotationsPerItem: COCO-VQA: 10 answers per question, 3 questions per image; DAQUAR-consensus: average of 5 ground truth answers per question; DAQUAR: 3 annotators; COCO-QA: 4 annotators; Visual Genome: average of 17 QA pairs per image.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: NLP algorithm used to automatically generate QA pairs from COCO captions for COCO-QA. Word2vec used for computing similarity between question words and object labels in FDA model. Edge Boxes used for generating bounding box region proposals.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper notes that as of the article's writing, Visual Genome is the largest VQA dataset and no methods beyond author-established baselines have been evaluated on it. The VQA Dataset hosted a 2016 VQA Challenge workshop. No explicit versioning or deprecation policies are described.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: SYNTH-VQA human cartoon models span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.
rai:dataSocialImpact: VQA has potential applications as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images on the web and in the real world. It could also improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content, and be used for image retrieval without using image meta-data or tags.
rai:dataBiases: Language biases are pervasive: question-only models can achieve 49.6% accuracy on COCO-VQA without using images. Yes/no answers span about 38% of all COCO-VQA questions, with 59% answered 'yes.' Answering 'yes' to all yes/no questions yields 71% accuracy using AccuracyVQA. Natural image datasets have contextual biases (e.g., street scenes more likely to have dogs than zebras). DAQUAR contains exclusively indoor scenes. COCO-QA has only four question types limited to COCO caption content. VQA systems are sensitive to question phrasing. Attentive mechanisms may attend to biased regions rather than task-relevant regions.
rai:dataLimitations: DAQUAR is too small to train complex models and contains only indoor scenes with clutter and extreme lighting; human accuracy is only 50.2%. COCO-QA has grammatical errors and nonsensical questions due to NLP generation flaws, and only four question types with single-word answers. COCO-VQA contains subjective opinion-seeking questions without single objective answers, and questions that can be answered without the image. FM-IQA's automatic evaluation is intractable due to sentence-length answers. Visual Genome's long-tailed answer distribution makes open-ended evaluation challenging. Multiple-choice evaluation can be gamed by exploiting answer biases. Current datasets are not sufficient to evaluate whether an algorithm has truly solved VQA.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, and Validation of VQA algorithms. Benchmarking image understanding systems. Evaluating visual Turing test capabilities. Applications include aiding blind and visually impaired users, improving human-computer interaction, and image retrieval. The paper recommends mean per-question-type performance as a more meaningful evaluation metric than overall accuracy.
